issues.title: Review of draft-skyfire-oauth-using-kyapay-tokens-01
issues.author: abr5427
issues.body:
Hi,

Below is my review of "Using KYAPay Tokens" [USING-KYAPAY],
draft-skyfire-oauth-using-kyapay-tokens-01.

Summary
=======

Most of the comments below come down to three high-level issues.

1. The bearer token carries personal and payment data.

   The token is a signed JWT, not an encrypted one (Section 4.1). In
   [KYAPAY-TOKEN], hid requires email and may carry name and phone, and
   sti carries settlement details. Anyone who sees the header during
   its lifetime can read the data and replay the token anywhere within
   its aud. Every hop that terminates TLS (CDN, WAF, bot manager,
   origin) sees it. Sections 5.1 and 9.3 answer this with "MUST NOT log
   or forward", which cannot be enforced or checked.

2. Admission without challenge.

   Section 6.3 says a bot manager "SHOULD admit the request ... rather
   than subjecting it to bot-blocking challenges." Combined with point
   1, a captured or cheaply obtained token becomes an open gate at the
   bot manager. Section 7.2 allows "progressive" verification that
   starts with only an email check, so "verified human" can mean very
   little. I don't have a good solution here, since the goal of the
   draft is easy adoption using the existing OAuth and JWT framework.

3. Some things to clarify to avoid implementation divergence.

   a. How intermediaries learn the aud set. Section 6.1 says to check
      that the token is "intended for this recipient", but an
      intermediary is not the recipient; the Target is. How will the
      intermediary know the audience set?

   b. Single-use vs. reusable. Section 8.3 asks for jti replay
      detection, while Section 4.3 validates "once (per session)" and
      mnr implies multiple requests.

   c. What the human authorized. Section 6.6 treats a valid token as
      evidence of a legitimate session, but the token does not name an
      account or an action. Is hid meant to equal the account? Nothing
      in the draft says so. Again this goes back to proof of
      possession.

Security comments
=================

S1. The token does not say which account it is for (Sections 6.6, 6.7,
    8.8)

A valid token with hid = attacker@example can be presented while
logging into, or acting on, someone else's account. Section 6.6 says an
ATO protector "SHOULD treat a validated KYAPay token ... as evidence
that a session is a human-initiated agentic session." That is true, but
it can be misread as evidence that the session is legitimate for this
account. The authors have said there is no low-burden way to bind the
token to an account today, and I agree.

Suggestion:

- Add a normative statement to 6.6 and 6.7, for example: "A KYAPay
  token attests the identity of the principal who authorized the agent.
  It does not convey authority over any account at the Target. ATO
  protectors and CIAM systems MUST NOT treat a validated token as
  authorization to access an account unless the token's principal has
  been linked to that account."

- One possible path that keeps intermediary burden low is a DPoP change
  I proposed on this list [DPOP-PROXY], which lets intermediaries
  validate both the token and the sender.

S2. Admission without challenge should depend on assurance (Sections
    6.2, 6.3, 7.2)

Section 6.3 says a bot manager "SHOULD admit the request ...
rather than subjecting it to bot-blocking challenges." Section 7.2
allows verification to begin with an email check. A bearer token
obtained with a throwaway email then bypasses bot defenses on login,
sign-up and checkout.

Suggestion. Make the admission SHOULD conditional: "...SHOULD admit the
request when the assurance levels in the token (Section 6.2) meet the
Target's policy for the requested action." Add that per-hid, per-aid
and per-apd rate and abuse limits still apply, and that sensitive
actions MAY still be challenged.

S3. Say the token is reusable, and drop jti replay detection (Sections
    4.1, 4.3, 8.3)

The token is meant to be reused within its roughly 5-minute lifetime.
Section 4.3 validates it "once (per session)" and the payment
claim mnr allows multiple requests. Yet Section 8.3 says verifiers
"SHOULD use the jti claim to detect replay." That can't work in
practice:

- A Target is usually fronted by many intermediary instances (PoPs,
  proxy fleets). Sharing jti state among them within the latency budget
  in 6.3 ("no per-request callout") is not realistic.

- Even a single-use token can't be enforced. Section 3.4 has the bot
  manager, fraud manager, ATO protector and CIAM system all validate
  the same token on the same request. Each layer would see the others'
  use as a replay.

Suggestion.

- State in 4.1 that the token is reusable within its lifetime and aud.

- List in-window replay within the aud set as an accepted risk of the
  bearer model.

- Reword 8.3 so jti is used for correlation, audit and issuer feedback
  (6.10), not replay detection.

- Point to proof of possession (4.3) as the only real fix, subject to
  S8 below.

S4. Define how intermediaries get the aud set (Sections 5.3, 6.1 step 5)

Issue. aud works like a store-restricted gift card: the issuer limits
which Targets can accept the token. An intermediary, though, is not the
audience. Section 6.1 step 5 ("intended for this recipient") gives it
no way to know which aud values are valid for the hosts it protects.
Multi-tenant intermediaries front many Targets. How aud relates to tdm
and tsi is also not stated.

Suggestion.

- Say that intermediaries obtain the acceptable aud (and tdm/tsi)
  values per protected Target through configuration, for example as
  part of each trusted issuer's configuration, and check the token
  against that set.
- Define the relationship between aud, tdm and tsi.
- Say how an agent determines the aud for a given Target.

S5. Check the issuer before fetching keys (Section 6.1 steps 3 and 4)

Step 3 verifies the signature against the issuer's key set before
step 4 checks that the issuer is trusted. Keys are found at
iss + /.well-known/jwks.json, so a literal reading has verifiers
fetching keys from any URL an attacker puts in iss (server-side request
forgery, denial of service). Well-built verifiers already allowlist
issuers, but the text should say so.

Suggestion.
Swap steps 3 and 4. Add: "A verifier MUST NOT retrieve key material
for an issuer that is not in its configured set of trusted issuers."

S6. Algorithm rules and token count (Sections 5.1, 6.1, References)

The draft sets no algorithm rules. JWT Best Current Practices
[RFC8725] is only an informative reference.

Suggestion.

- Make [RFC8725] a normative reference.
- Require verifiers to use an algorithm allowlist tied to each issuer's
  keys, and to reject "none" and symmetric algorithms.
- In 5.1, let recipients reject a header with more than one token per
  typ (at most 3 tokens). This caps verification cost per request.

S7. Token leakage through the agent's runtime (Section 8)

Tokens can leak through LLM transcripts, tool logs, and prompt
injection. Section 7.1 mentions keeping credentials from the LLM, but
Section 8 does not cover the threat. Proposed text is in the "Proposed
text: new Section 8.x" part at the end of this message.

S8. The planned proof-of-possession path reintroduces the rewriting
    problem (Section 4.3)

The bearer design is right not to depend on end-to-end request signing
such as Web Bot Auth. Signing the request's components is heavy, and
requests are routinely changed on the way to the origin. URL rewriting
is common, and sites deliberately keep external and internal URLs
separate so they don't expose internal architecture. When the signed
request is what the client sent, every proxy that rewrites the request
breaks verification or has to be given special handling.

In Section 4.3 the issuer binds the agent's public key into the
token (cnf), and the agent then signs each request, "a signature over
the request (method, path, body digest, timestamp/nonce) using
[RFC9421]", which is verified against cnf. The draft prefers this over
a detached, DPoP-style proof [RFC9449]. Because the signature covers
the path, the same rewriting fragility the bearer model avoids comes
back: an intermediary that rewrites the URL, or an origin that sees
only the internal path, can no longer verify it. Section 4.3 also notes
that stopping replay of the signature "requires either per-Target nonce
caches or binding the signature to the request content". That is the
same shared-state problem across distributed intermediaries described
in S3.

Suggestion.

- Make the rationale explicit in 4.2 and 4.3: why whole-request signing
  is avoided, including the URL rewriting and internal/external URL
  separation points above.
- For the proof-of-possession path, say which components are covered,
  and require a set that survives normal proxying. Alternatively, allow
  verification at the first intermediary, before any rewrite.
- Consider a DPoP-style proof designed for intermediaries as an
  alternative. My DPoP proposal on this list [DPOP-PROXY] addresses
  exactly this for URI-rewriting reverse proxies.

Privacy and PCI comments
========================

Sending the JWT in the clear is a reasonable choice: it reuses existing
OAuth/JWT infrastructure and keeps integration simple. The comments
below keep that model. They change what goes in the token, not how it
is carried.

P1. Replace personal data with a per-Target pseudonymous identifier
    (Sections 9.1, 9.3; hid in [KYAPAY-TOKEN])

hid requires email and may carry name and phone. Every intermediary
receives it (9.3), and the same email reaches every Target, which
lets sites track a person across all of them. Intermediaries don't
need this data: bot, fraud and ATO decisions (6.3 to 6.6) need a
stable handle and assurance levels, not a name or email.

Suggestion.

- Carry an opaque, pseudonymous principal identifier that differs per
  Target (pairwise, derived per aud), plus the verification and
  assurance sub-claims.
- A Target that needs the personal data (for example CIAM account
  creation in 6.7) gets it from the issuer out of band, authenticated
  as that Target, similar to the UserInfo endpoint in OpenID Connect
  Core 1.0 [OIDC], Section 5.3.

- Intermediaries can still rate-limit per principal, scope mitigations
  (6.9) and send feedback (6.10) using the pseudonym.

- Only the Target makes an issuer call, and only when it needs the
  data, so the "no per-request callout" property in 6.3 holds for
  intermediaries.

P2. Keep payment data out of the token (Section 6.4; sti in
    [KYAPAY-TOKEN])

If sti can contain card-related data, every hop that sees the
header may fall under PCI rules. Intermediary vendors and CDNs are
unlikely to accept that.

Suggestion.
Apply the P1 pattern: sti carries a reference that the Target
redeems with the issuer or payment processor. Add: "A KYAPay
token MUST NOT contain primary account numbers or other cardholder
data." Amount, currency and limits (amt, cur, mnr) can stay, since
fraud managers use them (6.4).

P3. Make aid.creation_ip optional ([KYAPAY-TOKEN])

Issue. creation_ip is REQUIRED. It is personal data, and Section 6.3
already says network-origin claims are "a weak corroborating signal
only."

Suggestion. Make it OPTIONAL.

Protocol and compatibility comments
===================================

C1. Header grammar and Structured Fields disagree (Sections 5.1, 10.1)

Section 5.1 defines its own ABNF, while 10.1 registers KYAPay-Token as
a Structured Field of type List. Under Structured Field Values for HTTP
[RFC9651], a malformed member makes the whole field fail to parse. That
conflicts with 5.1's "MUST ignore a member it cannot parse ... while
continuing to process the remaining members." Pick one: define the
field as an sf-list of sf-string (or sf-token) and drop the custom
ABNF, or drop the Structured Field registration.

C2. Header size (Section 5.1)

Up to three JWTs carrying identity and payment claims can exceed common
header limits (nginx header buffers, load balancer and CDN caps). Give
a recommended maximum field size, or at least a note. The P1 and P2
changes would shrink tokens considerably.

C3. Browser agents and CORS (Sections 3.3, 5.1)

A custom request header on a cross-origin fetch triggers a CORS
preflight. Page scripts can't send it unless the site allows it in
Access-Control-Allow-Headers. Browser-use agents also can't easily add
headers to page navigations. Say which requests carry the token
(top-level navigations, API calls, sub-resources), and qualify the
"zero merchant tech lift" claim for browser-based agents.

C4. No challenge or error response (Sections 6.5, 8.8)

A Target cannot signal "token required", "token rejected" or "higher
assurance needed." For step-up, which 6.5 lists as open, consider
reusing OAuth 2.0 Step Up Authentication Challenge Protocol [RFC9470],
which already defines WWW-Authenticate challenges for insufficient
authentication. It would also help to explain why the draft uses a new
header rather than an Authorization scheme (presumably to avoid
clashing with the site's own authentication).

Proposed text: new Section 8.x, Token Exposure in the Agent Runtime
===================================================================

Suggested for insertion after Section 8.5 (Compromised Agent Host). It
complements 8.5: that section covers malware using the agent's key,
while this one covers the token leaving the agent through its own
normal operation.

   8.x. Token Exposure in the Agent Runtime

   Agents driven by language models process untrusted content and
   record their activity in ways that conventional HTTP clients do not.
   A KYAPay token can therefore leave the agent through normal
   operation, without the agent host being compromised. Examples
   include:

   o  the token appearing in model context, conversation transcripts,
      or tool-call inputs and outputs that are logged, retained, or
      sent to a model provider;

   o  agent tracing, observability, or debugging systems that record
      outbound request headers;

   o  prompt injection, where content retrieved from a website or tool
      instructs the agent to reveal the token or to include it in a
      request to a party other than the intended Target.

   For a bearer token (Section 4.1), anyone who obtains a leaked token
   can use it at any audience in its aud until it expires. Audience
   binding does not help if the attacker presents the token at a
   legitimate Target.

   Agent developers and KYAPay Token Issuers SHOULD mint and attach
   tokens in deterministic components (Section 7.1) whose outputs are
   not placed in model context. Agents SHOULD attach a token only to
   requests whose destination matches the token's audience (aud, and
   tdm or tsi where used), and the component that attaches it MUST
   make that decision without relying on model output. Agent runtimes
   MUST NOT record KYAPay token values in logs, traces, or
   transcripts. Agents SHOULD request a new token for each Target and
   task rather than reusing one broadly, and SHOULD request the
   shortest lifetime that fits the task. Proof of possession (Section
   4.3) reduces this exposure only if the private key is also kept out
   of model context.

References
==========

[USING-KYAPAY]
   Agarwal, A., Jones, M. B., and S. Thumma, "Using KYAPay Tokens",
   draft-skyfire-oauth-using-kyapay-tokens-01,
   https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-skyfire-oauth-using-kyapay-tokens/
   Editor's copy:
   https://skyfire-xyz.github.io/draft-skyfire-oauth-using-kyapay-tokens/draft-skyfire-oauth-using-kyapay-tokens.html

[KYAPAY-TOKEN]
   Agarwal, A. and M. B. Jones, "KYAPay Token",
   draft-skyfire-oauth-kyapay-token-01,
   https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-skyfire-oauth-kyapay-token-01

[DPOP-PROXY]
   Allam, B., DPoP proposal for URI-rewriting reverse proxies, message
   to the OAuth WG mailing list,
   https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/oauth/F-UUNUUuZJihx_Qpms6EGsItoyc/

[RFC8725]
   Sheffer, Y., Hardt, D., and M. Jones, "JSON Web Token Best Current
   Practices", BCP 225, RFC 8725,
   https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8725

[RFC9421]
   Backman, A., Ed., Richer, J., Ed., and M. Sporny, "HTTP Message
   Signatures", RFC 9421,
   https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9421

[RFC9449]
   Fett, D., Campbell, B., Bradley, J., Lodderstedt, T., Jones, M., and
   D. Waite, "OAuth 2.0 Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP)",
   RFC 9449,
   https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9449

[RFC9470]
   Bertocci, V. and B. Campbell, "OAuth 2.0 Step Up Authentication
   Challenge Protocol", RFC 9470,
   https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9470

[RFC9651]
   Nottingham, M. and P-H. Kamp, "Structured Field Values for HTTP",
   RFC 9651,
   https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9651

[OIDC]
   Sakimura, N., Bradley, J., Jones, M., de Medeiros, B., and C.
   Mortimore, "OpenID Connect Core 1.0",
   https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html

Thanks,
Bhasker Allam

comments.body:
Thanks for your review and your suggestions, Bhasker.

Our replies are below, point by point in your order. This comment covers S1 to S8, and the next one covers P1 to P3 and C1 to C4. Where we're changing a draft, the proposed text is included. We'll open pull requests for these changes and link them here as they go up.

A few things have also changed in the editor's copies since the versions you reviewed, which may help when reading:

- `apd` and `aid.id` are now REQUIRED in the token draft;
- an agent's name must be unique among an agent platform's agents at a given issuer;
- token Section 4.1.3 sets clock-skew limits for `exp` and `iat` (at least 5 seconds, at most 60, with 30 recommended);
- the token draft now defines the `cnf` claim for proof of possession.

---

### S1. The token does not say which account it is for

We agree, and we'd like to take your suggested statement nearly as written. The Section 6.3 rewrite in -01 separated identification from admission for bot managers. But 6.6 and 6.7 can still be read as if a valid token stood in for account authorization, which is the confusion you describe.

We'd also like to update what we said earlier about there being no low-burden way to bind the token to an account. There is one that works today, and the draft should describe it. With the new default in P1, it has two steps:

- **The first time the agent signs in or creates an account,** the Target asks for the identifier its accounts are keyed on, usually an email address or phone number, through the decline response (C4). The issuer includes it only once the person has agreed, to the issuer or to the agent platform acting for it, and only if it has verified that the person controls it. How it verifies control is up to the issuer: a one-time code, a magic link, silent authentication on the phone, or another method. The Target compares it with the account and, if they match, records the token's hid.id against the account.
- **After that,** the Target can match on hid.id alone. hid.id is stable for that person on that agent platform at that Target service, so later sign-ins don't need the email again.

A match is evidence of control, not just knowledge. Anyone can type an email address, but only the person who controls it can pass the issuer's verification.

This is a check at the boundary, not on every request. It applies when the token is used to get into an account: sign-in, account creation, or exchange for an access token. Once the agent is inside the account, the KYA token is no longer the credential, as Section 6.6 already says.

On the DPoP route you mention, we've replied under S8.

Four changes:

**1. Section 2.1, "Human-via-agent request", appended:**

> The principal need not be present at the time of the request: the agent may be acting on an instruction given earlier, or on a standing authorization that the agent itself triggers, for example on a price change or on a schedule.

**2. Section 6.6, appended after the existing bullets:**

> A KYAPay token attests the identity of the principal who authorized the agent. It does not convey authority over any account at the Target. An ATO protector MUST NOT treat a validated token, on its own, as evidence that the session is authorized for the account it is acting on.
>
> Where a KYAPay token is presented to gain access to an account (at sign-in, at account creation, or when the token is exchanged for an access token as described above), a recipient SHOULD check that the token's principal is linked to that account. The principal is linked when the account already records the token's hid.id, or when a verified identifier in hid matches the corresponding identifier registered on the account. A match is a strong positive signal that the agent is acting within its own principal's account, and a recipient MAY weight it accordingly. A mismatch SHOULD be treated as grounds for step-up (Section 6.5) rather than as conclusive. Because an issuer asserts an identifier only where it has verified that the principal controls it, a match is evidence of control rather than of mere knowledge.

**3. Section 6.7, one bullet appended:**

> A validated token identifies the principal who authorized the agent; it does not by itself convey authority over an existing account. A CIAM system MAY create a new account from a validated token, in which case the token's principal is the account holder by construction, and it SHOULD record the token's hid.id against the account. To admit an agent to an existing account, a CIAM system MUST additionally establish that the token's principal is linked to that account. Any of the following is sufficient: the account already records the token's hid.id; a verified identifier in hid matches the corresponding attribute registered on the account; or an existing session for that account authenticated by other means. A mismatch, or the absence of any link, SHOULD be treated as grounds for step-up (Section 6.5) rather than as conclusive. A validated token alone MUST NOT be treated as sufficient.

**4. Token draft, Section 3.3.1 (hid).** It currently ends "Additional sub-claims MAY be defined and used. The recipient MUST ignore any unrecognized sub-claims." It would read:

> Additional sub-claims MAY be defined and used, including further identifiers for the human principal where a Target requires them to recognize an account. An issuer MUST NOT assert an identifier it has not verified to be under the control of the human principal. This document does not prescribe how control is verified; a one-time code, a magic link and silent network authentication are examples. The recipient MUST ignore any unrecognized sub-claims.

This sits alongside the rule already in the token draft that verified, when present, MUST be true, because an issuer does not issue a token carrying unverified identity claims.

The existing 6.6 and 6.7 bullets that mention reading the email address from hid will change with the default in P1, since the email is there only when the Target asked for it.

A Target keyed on email or phone number is served by this today. Anything beyond that is left open for now.

---

### S2. Admission without challenge should depend on assurance

We agree, and -01 already went most of the way. The sentence you quoted from 6.3 is gone, and the section now separates identification from admission:

> "Settling identification, however, does not grant automatic access. Identification is distinct from admission: classifying a request as a verified agent simply provides authenticated context. The bot manager uses the token's verified identity layer -- the human principal (hid), the agent platform (apd), and the agent instance (aid) -- to select and evaluate the site's configured access policy to determine the final disposition (admit, rate-limit, require step-up, or deny) rather than applying bot-blocking challenges designed for unattended, unattributed automation."

Your other two suggestions are covered in the draft, though not in 6.3 itself.

- Section 6.2 asks recipients to apply per-entity, per-action policy and to require step-up for higher-risk actions.
- Section 6.9 covers throttling or blocking at the level of one person (hid), one agent (aid) or a whole platform (apd).

We'll add a sentence to 6.3 so a bot manager reading only that section gets it too.

On the throwaway email: a token whose identity was checked only by email says so in its assurance claims (verified, ivm and amr). A site's policy can treat it differently from one backed by document and biometric checks. With the new default in P1, the email itself isn't in the token either.

One sentence still points the other way, and we'll fix it: Section 3.2, which you didn't flag but which says much the same thing.

Two changes:

**1. Section 3.2, last sentence.**

Before:

> This goal can only be met if security intermediaries admit legitimate human-via-agent requests by default when a valid token is present.

After:

> This goal can only be met if security intermediaries admit legitimate human-via-agent requests without per-site setup when a valid token is present and the verified identity it carries meets the site's policy for the requested action (Section 6.3).

**2. Section 6.3, appended after the paragraph quoted above:**

> Per-entity rate and abuse limits (Section 6.9) continue to apply to admitted requests, and a site MAY still challenge, or require step-up (Section 6.5) for, sensitive actions.

---

### S3. Say the token is reusable, and drop jti replay detection

We agree with all four suggestions and would like to take them nearly as written.

The clearest reason is the one you start with: a token is legitimately presented on many requests within its lifetime. Section 4.3 validates it once per session, and mnr allows several requests. So a jti cache in even a single recipient would flag every request after the first. jti identifies the token, not the request.

We'd describe proof of possession a little more narrowly than "the only real fix". A captured signed request can still be replayed verbatim within its window. DPoP has the same limit, and RFC 9449 Section 11.1 handles it with a jti cache scoped to the target URI. What proof of possession does stop is a stolen token being used on its own, whether it came from a log, a transcript, a tracing system or a compromised hop. That's the threat your Section 8.x describes, and it's the strongest argument for it.

We'd also describe reuse as the usual case rather than the only one. A deployment that can mint a distinct token for each request shouldn't read this as a prohibition, and in that deployment a repeated jti does mean replay.

Changes:

**1. Section 4.1, appended:**

> A KYAPay token is reusable within its validity period and audience. Unless a recipient knows that the issuer issues a distinct token for each request, it MUST NOT treat repeated presentation of the same token, within that period and audience, as evidence of replay. Nothing here prevents an issuer from issuing a distinct token for each request where that is practical; this document describes the general case, in which a token is presented more than once.

**2. Section 8.3, replaced in full:**

> A bare bearer token can be replayed by anyone who captures it within its validity window. As deployed today (Section 4), KYAPay accepts this bounded in-window risk and mitigates rather than eliminates it: recipients MUST confirm that the token is intended for them, as described in Section 5.3, so that a token minted for one Target cannot be presented to another, and MUST keep accepted lifetimes short. In-window replay within the token's audience is an accepted risk of the bearer model. Because a conforming token is presented on many requests within its lifetime, a repeated jti is not by itself evidence of replay, and the claim is used for correlation, audit, and issuer feedback (Section 6.10) rather than for replay detection. Where a deployment issues a distinct token for each request, a repeated jti does carry that meaning; this document describes the general case, in which it does not. Where a token carries a proof-of-possession key (cnf [RFC7800]), recipients MUST additionally verify a per-request signature [RFC9421] over that key (Section 6.1). This stops a stolen token from being used on its own, turning an open-ended token-theft exposure into a bounded window in which a captured signed request could be replayed verbatim; it does not prevent that verbatim replay. Access tokens produced by token exchange (Section 6.6) SHOULD be sender-constrained ([RFC9449], [RFC8705]).

**3. The same correction in the four other places that say proof of possession removes replay, or that recipients de-duplicate on jti:**

- **Section 6.3, "Replay Resistance" bullet.** "…SHOULD additionally verify the per-request signature [RFC9421] against that key, which removes in-window replay exposure." becomes "…SHOULD additionally verify the per-request signature [RFC9421] against that key, which stops a stolen token being used on its own (Section 8.3)."
- **Section 4.3, the paragraph after the numbered steps.** "…and closes the in-window replay and malicious-Target-reuse risks of the bearer model (Section 8)." becomes "…and closes the malicious-Target-reuse risk of the bearer model and stops a stolen token being used on its own (Section 8)."
- **Section 4.3, step 3.** "Nor can it rely on continuity between tokens: where a target de-duplicates on jti to prevent replay, each token is fresh and must stand on its own." becomes "Nor can it rely on continuity between tokens: a recipient may meet any given token first, so each token must stand on its own."
- **Token draft, Section 3.1, jti.** "This claim can be used to detect replay attempts." becomes "This claim identifies the token, not the request. A token may be presented on more than one request within its lifetime, so a repeated jti is not by itself evidence of replay."

---

### S4. Define how intermediaries get the aud set

This is a real gap, and the draft should say all three things you ask for.

How the three claims relate: aud and tsi are identifiers the Token Issuer assigns. aud names the Target, and tsi the particular service under it, such as a website, an API or an MCP server. Only a Target that has onboarded to that issuer knows its own values. tdm is the Target's domain: it's public and needs no relationship with the issuer to interpret.

That gives an intermediary something it can always check without configuration: it knows the domains it protects, so it checks tdm. Where it acts for a Target that has onboarded, it can also be configured with that Target's aud and tsi values, as you suggest, and check those too.

Your comment also shows a gap in that model: tdm is OPTIONAL today, and Section 6.1 checks it only "if used", so an intermediary can't rely on it being there. We'd make it required whenever the Target is reached by a domain name.

On how an agent finds the aud for a Target: it doesn't need to. The agent tells the issuer which Target it's minting for, either by its domain or URL or by the service ID it found in the issuer's directory, and the issuer sets aud and tsi. What an agent can't know in advance is what a Target will require, and that's the discovery work we mention under C4.

Changes:

**1. Using Section 5.3, first paragraph replaced** (the sentence on transport and discovery mechanisms that follows it is kept):

> The aud and tsi claims are identifiers assigned by the Token Issuer (Section 3.1.1 of [I-D.skyfire-oauth-kyapay-token]); their values are known to a Target that has onboarded to that issuer and are not otherwise discoverable. The tdm claim names the Target's domain, is not issuer-specific, and requires no relationship with the issuer to interpret. A Target that has onboarded to an issuer MAY check any of the three, and a security intermediary acting for such a Target MAY be configured with that Target's aud and tsi values and check them. A recipient that has not onboarded, including a security intermediary acting for many Targets, SHOULD check at least that tdm names the domain it is protecting for that request; where tdm also names a host or a path, the recipient MAY check those too. tdm MUST be present in tokens whose Target is identified by a domain name.

**2. Token draft, Section 3.1 designators and a new Section 3.1.1, "Identifying the Target":**

- `aud` names the Target's combination of identities, mirroring `sub`.
- `tsi` becomes REQUIRED.
- `tdm` becomes REQUIRED where the Target is identified by a domain name.

The new section reads:

> Three claims identify the party a token was minted for, and they answer different questions.
>
> The "aud" claim is the counterpart, on the Target side, of "sub" on the initiating side, and it names the same three things. Where "sub" identifies the combination of identities the issuer has verified for the initiator (the human principal, the agent platform and the agent), "aud" identifies that combination for the Target: the Target's agent, the platform it runs on, and the human principal behind it.
>
> "Agent" is used broadly on the Target side. On the initiating side it is a program acting for a person. On the Target side it is whatever the initiator is dealing with, which may be a website, an API, an MCP server, or another agent.
>
> The "tsi" claim identifies the particular service offered under that Target agent: a website, an MCP server, an API endpoint, or another interface. A single "aud" may offer several.
>
> The Token Issuer assigns both, and both are present in every token it creates, so that it can account for the tokens it has issued. Their values are meaningful to the issuer and to a Target that has onboarded to it; onboarding is what allows a Target to interpret them, not what causes them to be set.
>
> The two sides differ in what stands behind them. The identities named in "sub" are verified by the issuer. Those named in "aud" and "tsi" are verified where the Target has onboarded to the issuer; where the issuer has no means of confirming the Target, they are its record of the Target that the initiator asserted it was minting for, and "tdm" carries the domain the initiator supplied.
>
> A recipient reads these claims accordingly. They bind a token to one Target and so limit where it can be presented, which holds in either case because the binding narrows the token rather than granting anything. A recipient MUST NOT read "tdm" alone as the issuer confirming the Target's identity.
>
> The "tdm" claim identifies a Target reached over a URL-based interface, such as a website or an HTTP API: at least its domain, and optionally its host and a path. Unlike "aud" and "tsi" it is not issuer-specific, so any recipient can interpret it without a relationship with the issuer. It is present in addition to "aud" and "tsi" where the Target is reached that way.
>
> "tdm" and "tsi" are alternates rather than duplicates: they name the same Target by different means, one publicly interpretable and one not. A recipient validates whichever it is in a position to interpret. A Target that has onboarded to the issuer checks "aud" and "tsi". A recipient that has not, including a security intermediary acting for many Targets, checks at least that "tdm" names the domain it is protecting for that request. Section 5.3 of [I-D.skyfire-oauth-using-kyapay-tokens] describes that choice.

**3. Token draft, Section 4.1.2, step 6:**

Before:

> 6. Validate the aud Claim - Ensure that the aud identifies the recipient as the intended audience.

After:

> 6. Validate the Audience - A recipient that has onboarded to the issuer ensures that aud and tsi identify it as the intended audience. A recipient that has not ensures at least that tdm names the domain it is protecting for the request (Section 3.1.1).

**4. Using Section 6.1, step 5:**

Before:

> 5. MUST confirm that the token is intended for this recipient by checking the aud claim (and, if used, the tdm and tsi claims) as described in Section 8.

After:

> 5. MUST confirm that the token is intended for this recipient, as described in Section 5.3.

**5. Using Section 4.1, the audience-binding bullet:**

Before:

> audience binding (aud, and where used tdm/tsi), so a token minted for one Target cannot be presented to another;

After:

> audience binding (Section 5.3), so a token minted for one Target cannot be presented to another;

**6. Using Section 6, introduction:** "validation of exp, iat, jti, aud, and env" becomes "validation of exp, iat, jti, the audience, and env".

---

### S5. Check the issuer before fetching keys

You're right that the text should say so. Your review quotes -00 here. In -01, Section 6.1 checks issuer trust at step 2, before any key retrieval, and gives the reason:

> "This check MUST precede any processing that resolves a value taken from the token, and in particular any network retrieval driven by the iss claim. Until the token has been verified, iss is supplied by the sender: resolving it before the issuer is known to be trusted would allow an unauthenticated request to cause an outbound fetch to an arbitrary URL of the sender's choosing."

We'd still like to add your sentence. -01 states an ordering, and a prohibition is easier to test against. Your comment also made us look at the token draft, which has the same ordering problem. Its Section 4.1.2 lists the signature check before the issuer check, and Using Section 6.1 defers to it. So we'll fix it there too.

Changes:

**1. Using Section 6.1, step 2, appended:**

> A recipient MUST NOT retrieve key material for an issuer that is not in its configured set of trusted issuers.

**2. Token draft, Section 4.1, a new opening paragraph:**

> A recipient MUST confirm that the iss claim names an issuer it trusts before it performs any step below that retrieves key material or otherwise depends on the issuer. A recipient MUST NOT retrieve key material for an issuer that is not in its configured set of trusted issuers. The set of trusted issuers is configured out of band and is not derived from the token.

**3. Token draft, Section 4.1.2, the first two steps swapped:**

> 1. Validate iss Claim - Ensure that the token's issuer is one the recipient trusts (Section 4.1).
>
> 2. Verify JWT Signature - Valid JWTs MUST be signed with a valid key belonging to the token's issuer (iss claim).

**4. Token draft, Section 3.2 (Issuer Key Discovery), appended:**

> A recipient retrieves this JWK Set only for an issuer it trusts (Section 4.1).

---

### S6. Algorithm rules and token count

We agree with all three suggestions.

RFC 8725 should be normative in the Using draft. Section 8 already says implementers "MUST follow" it, so the reference section is inconsistent. We'll cite it as BCP 225 rather than by RFC number, since draft-ietf-oauth-rfc8725bis will obsolete RFC 8725 once it's published, and the BCP number carries over. The token draft already lists it as normative, but its prose says "SHOULD follow", so we'll align that too.

On algorithm rules, token -02 Section 4.1.1 already covers most of what you ask:
- alg must be present;
- an unsupported alg is rejected, including none;
- a token that would need an EC public key to be read as a symmetric key is refused;
- the JWK Set's alg and use parameters must match the token.

Re-reading it after your comment, we found one real gap. ES256 is only RECOMMENDED, and rejection is keyed on "not supported by both parties", so no algorithm is guaranteed to be common. An issuer using RS256 and a recipient supporting only ES256 would both be conformant and still couldn't interoperate. We'll set ES256 as a floor, tie the accepted set to the issuer's configuration and keys as you suggest, and say plainly that none and symmetric algorithms are rejected.

On the token count: Section 5.1 already asks senders not to send more than one token of the same typ. We'll add the receiving side as you suggest, so a recipient may reject a request that does, which caps a request at three tokens. Header size, the other half of this, is under C2.

Changes:

**1. Using Section 11:** [RFC8725] moves from Informative to Normative References, cited as BCP 225.

**2. Token draft, Section 5.1:**

Before:

> When validating the JWTs described in this specification, implementers SHOULD follow the best practices and guidelines described in [RFC8725].

After:

> When validating the JWTs described in this specification, implementers MUST follow the JSON Web Token Best Current Practices, BCP 225 [RFC8725].

**3. Token draft, Section 4.1.1, item 1, replaced:**

> The alg header parameter MUST be present. Recipients MUST support ES256 [RFC7518]; issuers SHOULD use ES256.
>
> A recipient MUST determine the set of algorithms it will accept for a given issuer from its own configuration and from that issuer's JWK Set, and MUST NOT derive that set from the token. A token whose alg value is absent from, or outside, that set MUST be rejected, including the value none [RFC7515] and any symmetric (MAC) algorithm, since an issuer's JWK Set publishes only public keys. Verification is then performed using the algorithm named in the token and the key obtained from the issuer's JWK Set (item 2), or the token is rejected. In particular, a recipient MUST NOT accept a token that would require interpreting an Elliptic Curve public key as a symmetric key.
>
> Requiring support for ES256 guarantees that any conforming issuer and recipient share at least one algorithm, without constraining which algorithm a deployment uses. Implementations remain free to support and use others, including post-quantum algorithms as they are standardized; this requirement is a floor for interoperability, not a ceiling on agility.

(The existing paragraph requiring the JWK Set's alg and use parameters to be consistent with the token stays as it is.)

**4. Using Section 5.1, one bullet added to the recipient list:**

> MAY reject a request that carries more than one token of the same typ.

---

### S7. Token leakage through the agent's runtime

Thanks for writing this section, Bhasker. We'd like to add it after Section 8.5 as you suggest, close to your wording, and credit you for the text. It sits well next to 8.5: that section covers malware using the agent's key, and yours covers the token leaving the agent through its normal operation.

We'd make three small edits, and one matching change in the token draft.

The bearer sentence. With the change under S4, a token is bound to the one Target it was minted for, so a leaked token "can be presented at the Target it was minted for until it expires".

The attach rule. As under S4, aud and tsi are values the issuer assigns, and an agent can't always interpret them. What the agent does know is the Target it asked the issuer for. So the component that attaches the token checks the destination against that Target, and against tdm where the token carries one.

The logging rule. "MUST NOT record KYAPay token values in logs, traces, or transcripts" works for logs and traces. For transcripts, it doesn't fit how many agents get tokens today, ours included. When an agent gets a token by calling a tool, such as an MCP tool, the tool result goes back to the model. The token is then in model context, and any transcript the runtime keeps contains it. Your first SHOULD allows for that case, and the MUST NOT would then rule it out. So we'd split it by what a runtime controls:

- a MUST NOT for logs, traces and observability exports. This matters, because LLM tracing tools commonly record tool inputs and outputs, some of them by default;
- where a token reaches model context anyway, a SHOULD to treat it as disclosed to everyone with access to that context, including the model provider. Short-lived, per-Target tokens are then the main mitigation, along with proof of possession where the private key is held outside model context.

The token draft's Section 5.2 already says tokens MUST NOT be written to logs or other persistent stores not required to process the transaction. We'll align it with this split so the two drafts agree.

Separately, with the change under P1 a token carries hid.id by default rather than an email address, so a leaked token also gives away less.

Changes:

**1. Using, new Section 8.6, after Section 8.5** (today's 8.6 to 8.9 become 8.7 to 8.10):

> 8.6. Token Exposure in the Agent Runtime
>
> Agents driven by language models process untrusted content and record their activity in ways that conventional HTTP clients do not. A KYAPay token can therefore leave the agent through normal operation, without the agent host being compromised. Examples include:
>
> * the token appearing in model context, conversation transcripts, or tool-call inputs and outputs that are logged, retained, or sent to a model provider;
>
> * agent tracing, observability, or debugging systems that record outbound request headers;
>
> * prompt injection, where content retrieved from a website or tool instructs the agent to reveal the token or to include it in a request to a party other than the intended Target.
>
> For a bearer token (Section 4.1), anyone who obtains a leaked token can present it at the Target it was minted for until it expires. Audience binding (Section 5.3) does not help if the attacker presents the token at that Target.
>
> Agent developers and KYAPay Token Issuers SHOULD mint and attach tokens in deterministic components (Section 7.1) whose outputs are not placed in model context. Agents SHOULD attach a token only to requests sent to the Target for which the token was requested; where the token carries tdm, that means a destination within the domain that tdm names. The component that attaches a token MUST make that decision without relying on model output.
>
> Agent runtimes MUST NOT write KYAPay token values to logs, traces, or observability exports.
>
> Agents SHOULD request a new token for each Target and task rather than reusing one broadly, and SHOULD request the shortest lifetime that fits the task. Proof of possession (Section 4.3) reduces this exposure only if the private key is also kept out of model context.
>
> Some architectures place a token in model context unavoidably. Where an agent obtains a token by invoking a tool, the tool result is returned to the model, and any retained transcript of that session therefore contains the token. A deployment in that position SHOULD treat the token as disclosed to every party with access to that context, including the model provider. For such a deployment, per-Target, short-lived tokens are the main mitigation, together with proof of possession where the private key is held outside model context.

**2. Token draft, Section 5.2, the logging bullet**:

Before:

> Tokens MUST NOT be written to logs, analytics pipelines, or other persistent stores that are not required to process the transaction.

After:

> Tokens MUST NOT be written to logs, traces, analytics pipelines, or other persistent stores that are not required to process the transaction. An agent that obtains a token through a tool whose result is returned to a language model may be unable to keep the token out of that model's context or out of a transcript retained from it; Section 8.6 of [I-D.skyfire-oauth-using-kyapay-tokens] describes how such a deployment treats the token.

---

### S8. The planned proof-of-possession path reintroduces the rewriting problem

We agree the rationale belongs in the draft, and we'll add it to Sections 4.2 and 4.3, including your point about sites keeping their external and internal URLs separate.

You're right that Section 4.3 reads as if the signature covers the path the origin sees. The parenthetical "(method, path, body digest, timestamp/nonce)" was meant as an illustration. The draft already requires a recipient to verify an RFC 9421 signature when a token carries cnf (Sections 4.3, 6.1 and 8.3), but it never says which components that signature covers. RFC 9421 Section 1.4 leaves that choice to each profile, so it's ours to make, and the draft should make it.

We'd take the second option you suggest: verify at the first intermediary, before any rewrite. That's the CDN, bot manager or edge worker that receives the request as the agent sent it, and it's where KYAPay verification already happens. Where that hop rewrites the request itself, it verifies first. It doesn't forward a request that fails the check, so the layers behind it can rely on it, as long as requests can't go around it. They still validate the token, which a rewrite doesn't change. None of this changes the default: proof of possession stays optional, and a token without a cnf key is handled as a bearer token, as today.

With verification at the first hop, the covered set doesn't have to survive proxying, so we'd keep it complete: `@method`, `@target-uri`, content-digest whenever the request has a body, and the KYAPay-Token field, so that a signature can't be presented beside a different token. A smaller set would mostly change which deployments fail. Without the path, a captured signature could be used at another path on the same host, and `@authority` on its own breaks under host rewriting in the same way the path does under path rewriting.

We also looked at having the rewriting proxy pass the original URI along. Forwarded (RFC 7239) has no path parameter, and its Section 8.1 says the field "cannot be relied upon to be correct", so it can't be what a signature is checked against.

On replay, you're right that the nonce-cache sentence in 4.3 leads back to the S3 problem, and we don't plan to rely on a cache. As under S3, the covered set stops a captured signature being altered or used with another request, and created and expires bound how long an identical request could be resent. We'll reword that sentence to say so.

On your DPoP proposal: it takes the other route, making htm and htu optional so a proof survives rewriting. For KYAPay we'd rather keep the request binding and verify at the first hop. Your Section 3.4 describes that pattern for Transaction Tokens, where the proof "only needs to survive the one external hop where the URI is still unchanged", with a Transaction Token Service at each trust boundary. You also note that verifying before the rewrite makes the proxy the terminal verifier. In KYAPay the bot manager or CDN in front of the Target already verifies the token (Section 6.3), so the pattern needs no new infrastructure or role. Without htu, protection against verbatim replay would also fall to a jti cache, which runs into the shared-state problem you describe under S3.

The rest of the profile (the source of the verification key, the keyid and tag parameters, error responses and a worked example) is written, and we'll bring it into the draft as its own pull request once co-authors have reviewed it.

Changes:

**1. Using Section 4.2, a new closing paragraph:**

> A KYA token is verified the same way however a request is routed, because it is a self-contained JWT and not a signature over the request. A signature over the request is different: it can be verified only where the request still has the form the agent signed. Requests are routinely rewritten on the way to an origin. CDNs, load balancers, API gateways and edge workers add or strip path prefixes, route to internal host names and normalize URIs, and sites deliberately keep their external and internal URLs separate so as not to expose their internal architecture. A design in which every recipient verified a signature over the request would fail at each such hop, or need special handling there. This is why KYA is a bearer token by default (Section 4.1), and why, where proof of possession is used, the request signature is verified at the first hop (Section 4.4).

**2. Using Section 4.3, step 4:**

Before:

> 4. the agent signs each request in place -- a signature over the request (method, path, body digest, timestamp/nonce) using [RFC9421] -- verified against the key in cnf, with no separate proof-of-possession token.

After:

> 4. the agent signs each request in place using [RFC9421], covering the components listed in Section 4.4, and the signature is verified against the key in cnf, with no separate proof-of-possession token.

**3. Using Section 4.3, last paragraph, the replay sentence:**

Before:

> Defeating replay of the proof itself further requires either per-Target nonce caches or binding the signature to the request content, and other request-bound designs considered (mutual TLS [RFC8705], TLS channel binding, session-based schemes) each raise the participation bar or add Target-side state.

After:

> Binding the signature to the request (Section 4.4) stops a captured signature from being altered or presented with a different request; an identical request can still be resent until the signature expires, and this document does not rely on per-Target nonce caches to prevent that (Section 8.3). Other request-bound designs considered (mutual TLS [RFC8705], TLS channel binding, session-based schemes) each raise the participation bar or add Target-side state.

**4. Using, new Section 4.4, "Request Signatures for Proof of Possession":**

> Where a token carries a proof-of-possession key (Section 4.3), the agent signs each request with that key using HTTP Message Signatures [RFC9421]. The signature MUST cover:
>
> * the `@method` derived component;
>
> * the `@target-uri` derived component;
>
> * the KYAPay-Token header field, so that a signature cannot be presented with a different token; and
>
> * the Content-Digest header field [RFC9530], whenever the request has content.
>
> The signature MUST carry the created and expires parameters.
>
> Proof of possession is optional. A token that carries no proof-of-possession key is a bearer token (Section 4.1), and nothing in this section applies to it.
>
> A covered component has to hold the same value when the signature is verified as when it was created, and a hop that rewrites a request changes the components that say where it is going. The signature is therefore verified by the first recipient to receive the request as the agent sent it, before any rewriting, which is usually the CDN, bot manager, or edge worker in front of the Target. A recipient that rewrites a request MUST verify the signature before rewriting it. The recipient that verifies the signature MUST NOT forward a request whose signature is absent or invalid; it rejects the request (Section 6.1). A recipient behind that hop MAY rely on it instead of verifying the signature itself, but only where the deployment ensures that requests cannot reach it without passing through that hop. It still validates the token as described in Section 6.1.
>
> The other elements that Section 1.4 of [RFC9421] requires a profile to specify, including the source of the verification key, the keyid and tag parameters, and error responses, are expected to be specified in a future revision of this document.

**5. Using Section 6.1, step 6 split in two.** The signature rule moves out of the env step into a step of its own; today's steps 7 and 8 become 8 and 9. Nothing refers to them by number.

Before (step 6):

> 6. MUST confirm that the env claim (for example, production) matches the environment the intermediary is operating in. When the token carries a proof-of-possession key (the cnf claim [RFC7800], Section 4), MUST verify that the request is signed by that key -- over HTTP, using HTTP Message Signatures [RFC9421] -- and reject the request if the signature is absent or invalid.

After (steps 6 and 7):

> 6. MUST confirm that the env claim (for example, production) matches the environment the intermediary is operating in.
>
> 7. When the token carries a proof-of-possession key (the cnf claim [RFC7800], Section 4.3), MUST verify that the request is signed by that key as described in Section 4.4, and MUST reject the request, and not forward it, if the signature is absent or invalid. An intermediary behind a hop that has already done so MAY rely on that hop instead, as Section 4.4 describes. When the token carries no such key, this step does not apply.

**6. Using Section 6.3, the "Replay Resistance" bullet, second sentence** (as amended under S3):

Before:

> Where a token carries a proof-of-possession key (Section 4), the bot manager (or the edge/CDN provider acting for the Target) SHOULD additionally verify the per-request signature [RFC9421] against that key, which stops a stolen token being used on its own (Section 8.3).

After:

> Where a token carries a proof-of-possession key (Section 4.3), the per-request signature is verified at the first hop, before any rewriting, which is usually the bot manager or the edge/CDN provider acting for the Target (Section 4.4); this stops a stolen token being used on its own (Section 8.3).

**7. Using Section 8.3** (the approved S3 replacement), one pointer: "recipients MUST additionally verify a per-request signature [RFC9421] over that key (Section 6.1)" becomes "…over that key (Section 4.4)".
